margin: Woburn, MA | October 2026 | A Solo Travelogue by Roddsi Sarkar, originally recorded as an 18 minute long voice note and later transcribed.
items.body:
Part I: Leaf Peeping, Aura Photography, and Lobster Rolls
I went to New England leaf peeping. I find it quite amusing that there's an established recreational activity where people travel hundreds of miles, sometimes across the country, to watch leaves change color. And there I was, doing exactly that. Four states in five days. I had escaped reality, San Jose, and landed in Boston with a fairly ambitious itinerary, which, in hindsight, was probably more of an endurance test than a vacation. But what are you doing in New England in October if you're not looking at the fall colors, right? My first stop was Salem. Salem was something I'd been looking forward to for quite some time. I've always been fascinated by magic, mythology, and supernatural things. But for me, something has to connect to reality. And Salem has that rather uncomfortable distinction of being a place where things we associate with fiction were once treated as matters of life and death. It was October 1, so naturally, there were costumes, decorations, and a Halloween parade. People were very much in the spirit of things. And I got my aura photographed. Yes. Fifty dollars to have someone tell me what colors my invisible energy field apparently contains. There were sensors, explanations about the solar plexus and heart, and interpretations of what the different colors supposedly meant. And the funny thing is, some of it matched. Or at least, I thought it matched. Which could mean something. Or it could simply mean that I was finding things that matched because I wanted them to. I also visited Nathaniel Hawthorne's birthplace, which was a very different experience. I'd had some run-ins with his books in our school library. I'd known a little about him but had never actually read his books cover to cover. And yet, after learning about his life and writing, I somehow ended up buying three copies of The Scarlet Letter. One for myself, two for my best friends from school. Friends I've known for over two decades. Why three copies of a book I haven't read? I don't know. There's something about being in possession of a book that makes me feel good. The idea that someday I'll read it. That it's there, waiting for me. I also got an Edgar Allan Poe book from a witchy store. Another author I was introduced to by one of those friends, through a tiny, dusty book in our school library.
The following day, I went on a tour of southern Vermont and western Massachusetts. I was expecting something extraordinary, and some of the stops were, well, fairly ordinary. There was a covered bridge. I mean, what's so fascinating about a covered bridge? It's a bridge. With a roof. Of course, I understand the historical and architectural significance. But I don't necessarily think every covered bridge warrants a photograph or a permanent place in one's memory. The Hogback Mountain overlook, however, was beautiful. That's where I could really see the fall colors–orange, yellow, hints of red, all mixed with green. It was different. And I was happy I'd gone. I'd also added two more states to my travel itinerary, which was admittedly part of the motivation. Sometimes we travel to experience places. Sometimes we travel to collect them. I was doing a bit of both. The next day was New Hampshire. The White Mountains. The Kancamagus Highway. North Conway. I wish my eyes could simply remember what they saw. The colors were so bright. The reflections in the lakes and ponds were almost unreal. You could see the trees mirrored in the water, all those yellows and oranges, with the mountains in the background. It was breathtaking. Not quite Maui, though. Maui remains in a different category for me. I've never had that particular out-of-body feeling anywhere else. New Hampshire felt closer to Yosemite, but dressed for autumn. The only problem was that everyone else had apparently received the same memo about peak foliage. There were people everywhere. Which I understand, because I was one of those people. But sometimes the crowds made it difficult to take everything in. You'd find yourself looking at this extraordinary landscape while also trying to work out where to stand, how to take a photograph, and whether someone was about to walk into your frame. I also discovered hot apple cider. Apparently, everyone knows about hot apple cider. But for me, it felt fancy. And I had some apple cinnamon or maple donuts that were so soft they practically melted in my mouth. 
Portland, Maine was another kind of adventure. I took the Amtrak Downeaster from Boston. A little over two hours on a train, which was a nice change from spending an entire day being driven from one scenic overlook to another. There seemed to be some skateboarding event going on. I watched people doing these ridiculous, high-stakes tricks involving loops and things whose technical names I don't know. Impressive and potentially dangerous. I had a lobster roll. And tuna crudo, which was recommended by a lady sitting beside me at a bar overlooking the street. I'd never had it before. It's somewhat like sashimi. I sent pictures to my mom. She wasn't particularly fond of the raw fish situation, but she did give a heart reaction to the lobster roll. So I suppose that was the family approved culinary highlight. Then there was the potato donut. And finally, pain perdu. What a name for an ice cream. I later learned that pain perdu literally means "lost bread" in French, referring to what we commonly know as French toast. I found that quite funny. There I was, in Maine, having an ice cream named after bread that had apparently been lost and subsequently recovered as dessert. By this point, my New England trip had become a rather eclectic collection of experiences: leaf peeping, aura photography, witchy bookstores, historic bridges, scenic highways, lobster rolls, and an unusually large number of donuts. And yet, when I think about what stayed with me, it's not necessarily these experiences. It's the people who happened to be there.
Part II: Tête-à-Tête with Trees and Fellow Strangers
One thing that genuinely surprised me about this trip was how nice people were. And I don't mean that people are generally unkind. I think it's more that I don't always notice kindness. Or maybe I don't bother to notice it. I'm usually thinking about a thousand different things, making assumptions about people, or simply too preoccupied with whatever is happening inside my head to pay attention to what they're giving away. But something was different this time. Maybe traveling alone made me more observant. Or maybe it made me more welcoming. Not just to others, but to myself. On the Vermont and western Massachusetts tour, I met this wonderful older lady. She was traveling with a group of friends, all of whom were celebrating their 70th birthdays that year. They'd decided to go on a fifteen-day trip together. These were people who'd known each other for years, and here they were, traveling together, celebrating another year of their lives. She was sitting beside me on the bus and started asking the usual questions. How are you? What brings you here? Are you traveling alone? And we started talking. About the trip, about places, about different things. At some point, she even offered me a maple syrup-filled cookie. Such a small gesture. But I remember it. There's something very comforting about a stranger offering you food without expecting anything in return. It's an ordinary act of generosity, but perhaps not one we're accustomed to noticing.
There was also this Indian girl on the same tour. She was a Boston local exploring the area, and we ended up having lunch together. Then we spent almost two hours at the Yankee Candle store. Which is quite a long time to spend inspecting candles, now that I think about it. But it was fun. We talked about different things, shared recommendations, and had a good time. I don't know what to call that. A micro-short-term friendship? Never mind getting the taxonomy right. What struck me was how naturally we got along. You know that feeling when you meet someone and think, if circumstances were different, we could actually have been good friends? It was something like that. We weren't sitting together on the bus, and at one point, I got distracted talking to the tour guide. I didn't notice where she'd gone. But almost ten minutes later, she found me at the next block. She started giving me recommendations about Boston, where to eat, places around Faneuil Hall, and how to get back to my hotel. And I thought, wow, that's so nice. Unfortunately, I had exhausted what was probably the last bit of social energy I had for the day. I told her I was going to the waterfront, and that was how we parted. Which, in hindsight, was a little strange. I could have asked whether she wanted to walk together. Or accompany her to the station. Or continue the conversation. But I didn't. Maybe she wanted to be friends. Maybe she was simply being nice. I don't know. I keep returning to that exchange, wondering whether I should have done something differently. But perhaps that's the thing about these encounters. You don't always recognize their significance while they're happening. And by the time you do, the moment has already passed.
There was another elderly lady I met in Portland. We were standing in a queue outside a potato donut shop, debating which donut to get. At some point, we started wondering whether we should just order online. Which is a perfectly reasonable question, except that we were standing right in front of the store. We eventually decided against it. Because if you're going to visit a famous local donut shop, you should probably have the in-store experience. But I remember that conversation quite fondly. Two complete strangers temporarily united by the important matter of donut procurement. I don't know her name. I don't know where she was from. I'll probably never see her again. But I remember our little discussion. And then there was the woman at the Portland bar who recommended tuna crudo. We were just sitting next to each other, overlooking the street. She suggested something, I tried it, and that was that. No elaborate introduction. No exchange of contact details. Just a small, perfectly ordinary conversation. And yet, these are some of the moments I remember most clearly. I've been thinking about why that is. We tend to associate friendships with continuity. You meet someone, get to know them, exchange numbers, make plans, and keep in touch. But what about these other people? The ones you meet on a bus, in a queue, or at a bar? I find that oddly fascinating. You share a little part of your life with someone, knowing almost nothing about them, and then you both return to your respective worlds. Maybe there's a kind of freedom in that. You don't have to maintain anything. You don't have to worry about what happens next. You can just have a conversation. And move on. I wouldn't necessarily romanticize every interaction. But I think there's value in that, too. Not everything needs to become a friendship to have been meaningful. And this trip reminded me of something else. I'm usually very harsh on myself. I don't always know how to be generous to myself, let alone acknowledge when I'm doing something good. People kept telling me that I was brave for traveling alone across the country, staying in a hotel, taking Amtrak, and going on tours with random strangers. But I didn't really see it that way. When you're doing these things, you don't necessarily overthink them. You just go with the flow. Of course, you remain aware of your surroundings and make sensible decisions. But you also give yourself room to respond to situations instead of trying to anticipate everything. And maybe that was the difference. I was simply more available to the people around me. More importantly, perhaps I was more available to myself. That doesn't mean I came back transformed. I don't think five days of travel can magically resolve years of overthinking. But it did make me notice things I might otherwise have missed. And funnily enough, the people who made this trip memorable are mostly people I will probably never meet again. I went all the way to New England to chase leaves that were about to fall. Ironically, I ended up remembering people who were about to leave.
Part III: Binder Clips, Chair Edges, and Other Unresolved Mysteries
On the last day of my trip, I decided to stay in Boston. I'd originally considered going to Providence, Rhode Island, or perhaps Concord. Five states in five days has a certain appeal to it. At some point, I had to acknowledge that this was supposed to be a vacation, not an interstate travel event. I started with Harvard. The campus has that old world academic feeling. I walked around, visited the Harvard Book Store, saw the John Harvard statue, and spent some time exploring. Then I took the T to MIT. Where Harvard has that historic, almost literary character, MIT was all glass buildings and modern structures. I video called my parents and showed them around. "This is the dome. This is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology." There seemed to be some recruitment event involving OpenAI and Apple, or at least some information about internships. And I thought, wow. So this is where these companies come to find people. No wonder. You throw a stone toward some of these top AI companies, and there's a decent chance it'll land near someone from MIT, Harvard, or Stanford. Not literally, of course. But you get the idea. I was so busy showing everything to my parents that I forgot to take proper pictures. Which is funny because I'd traveled all this way, stood in front of MIT, and somehow failed at the basic tourist responsibility of documenting it. From MIT, I took the T to Beacon Hill. I visited this beautiful bookstore with a little café attached to it. And that's where I discovered Persephone Books. Now, I don't even know how to pronounce Persephone properly. But I was fascinated by the idea. This publisher brings neglected and out of print works back into circulation, particularly books written by women. And the books have these beautiful gray covers. Very understated. Very elegant. Naturally, I bought two. Another seventy dollars out of my wallet. There's something about holding a book, especially one with an interesting history. The fact that someone has taken the time to recover these neglected works, to make these authors heard again, even decades later–I find that quite moving. I might give one to a friend. I've already sent her a voice note suggesting she try something different.
The café beside the bookstore was lovely. You actually had to crouch a little to get in, and there was this small garden outside. I ordered fig pudding, which was amazing. Not excessively sweet at first, but by the end, I was struggling. I also ordered a mocktail which the staff suggested and it wasn't particularly good. And I remember wondering why nobody had suggested a cocktail when they clearly served alcohol. I could have said, "You know, I have an ID. I can take it out of my backpack." But that would have been a whole other conversation. And I was too tired. So I sat there with my fig pudding and disappointing mocktail, minding my own business. Because the tables were very close together, I could hear the conversation happening right beside me. There were two people having what seemed like a coffee chat. One appeared to be a student, possibly from MIT or Harvard. The other might have been a professor. But the student was doing most of the talking. And he was so articulate. They were talking about other students and some of the little habits people have. And I found it interesting how closely we observe one another without necessarily realizing it. Someone might scrunch their nose while looking at a menu. To that person, it's just a habit. To someone else, it's a distinct, recognizable mannerism. That made me think about something I'd noticed about myself earlier that day. I tend to sit on the edge of chairs. I noticed it at the café. And I suddenly thought, why? Why can't I just lean back? Maybe it's because I'm constantly trying to pay attention to whatever is in front of me. I'm always leaning forward. Trying to grab onto something. Trying to chase whatever is ahead. And not necessarily giving myself enough room to lean back or look back. Is that metaphorical? Perhaps. Or maybe I'm simply trying to stretch my limits. Which isn't necessarily a bad thing. I don't know why my brain insists on turning an ordinary seating preference into a question about my relationship with ambition. But there I was. Sitting on the edge of a chair. Anyway, coming back to the two people beside me. At some point, the student offered to pay the bill. And when he reached for his cards, I noticed something peculiar. He didn't have a wallet. He had a bunch of cards–university ID, credit cards, maybe a transportation card. And they were all held together by a binder clip. One of those little black clips you use to hold papers together. I thought that was brilliant. Absolutely brilliant. There's an entire industry dedicated to designing compact wallets. You have brands like Ridge making these sleek metal wallets, selling the idea of minimalism and clever engineering. And here's this student with a binder clip. I mean, of course, there are practical concerns. Your card numbers are exposed. Your CVV might be visible. You probably don't want to leave the whole thing unattended. But still. Such a simple solution. And I immediately thought, no wonder these kids are at MIT or Harvard which is a completely unreasonable conclusion to draw from someone's choice of wallet. The student might not even have attended either university. But in my head, the binder clip had already become evidence of intellectual ingenuity.
By the time I returned to my hotel, I was exhausted. I was contemplating going out for one last dinner in Boston, but I'd already had fig pudding, a mocktail, and another latte—a cinnamon bun latte, this time. I was full. And I had to wake up around 2:30 the following morning to catch my flight. I lay on my hotel bed and started recording my thoughts. Just talking. I simply wanted to remember things. Not just where I'd been, but what I'd noticed. And I think that's an important distinction. Because I wouldn't necessarily call this trip therapeutic. I was clocking twelve, fourteen, sometimes fifteen hours a day. Walking around, taking trains, getting on buses, navigating unfamiliar places, trying to fit everything into five days. That's not exactly a rest. But it was something I needed. I needed to be adventurous without necessarily doing anything dangerous. I needed to get away from the routine, meet people, try things, and realize that I could be perfectly content doing all of that by myself. I also needed to notice that there are people who are genuinely kind. And that perhaps I'm too preoccupied most of the time to appreciate it. I hope I can carry a little of this curiosity back with me. The willingness to talk to someone without expecting anything. The ability to find something amusing in the mundane. The realization that a brief interaction doesn't need a lasting relationship to deserve a place in my memory. And maybe I'll even learn to lean back in a chair occasionally. I went leaf peeping. But the binder clip, the maple syrup cookie, and the people I will probably never meet again might stay with me a little longer. Funny, isn't it?

Books stands tall, guarding secrets
The rest of us lean in for the beautiful lies
